info.title: Be a Meditator Today: Testing Identity-Based Message Framing for Meditation in a Digital Field Experiment

text.text: Objectives.
Brief in-app messages are commonly used to prompt meditation, but little is known about which message features influence engagement.

Drawing on the reasoned action approach and research on self-identity, this study tested whether framing meditation as an identity ("Be a meditator today") rather than a behavior ("Meditate today") increases engagement, and whether any effect depends on prior engagement.

In a randomized field experiment on Spotify, 3,000 U.S. adults who had recently listened to a popular meditation teacher received one of two in-app messages that differed only in identity versus behavior framing.
Outcomes were message click-through and listening to the teacher's content during the treatment period, analyzed by intent to treat.
Logistic regression tested moderation by prior listening.
Results.
Click-through did not differ between conditions (8.2% vs.
8.2%; difference = -0.05 percentage points, 95% CI [-2.03, 1.92]).
Identity framing did not increase listening during the treatment period (Mann-Whitney U = 1,106,605, p = .313; mean difference = 1.26 min, 95% CI [-5.72, 8.24]).
Prior listening (median split) did not moderate the effect of framing (interaction OR = 0.93, 95% CI [0.55, 1.56], p = .77).
Identity-based framing did not increase engagement, even among an audience for whom the meditator identity was plausible.
Consistent with the reasoned action approach, changing a message's grammatical form without changing the beliefs it makes salient may offer little leverage over behavior.
Preregistration.
This study was not preregistered.

Regular practice is central to how mindfulness and meditation are thought to produce their benefits, yet many people who try meditation do not develop a sustained practice, and retention in meditation apps is low (Baumel et al., 2019; Bowen & Beam, 2025; Kozlov et al., 2020).

text.text: Digital platforms routinely use messaging (e.g., in-app messages, email, push notifications, etc.) to initiate engagement, and because such messages are inexpensive and scalable, even small gains in their effectiveness could matter.

text.text: Intention follows from attitude toward the behavior, perceived norms, and perceived behavioral control.
These are based on accessible beliefs about the behavior's likely outcomes, what important others think and do, and the factors that make the behavior easier or harder to perform.
Actual control then moderates whether intentions are carried out.
From this perspective, a message can plausibly change behavior by influencing the beliefs that are salient when people decide whether to act (Fishbein & Ajzen, 2009).

text.text: Identity theorists, in contrast, argue that people act in line with their self-identities to verify their sense of who they are, a motive distinct from those captured by attitudes and norms (Rise et al., 2010).

text.text: Empirically, in a meta-analysis of 40 independent tests spanning behaviors such as exercise, healthy eating, and smoking, self-identity correlated with intention about as strongly as attitude did, explained an additional 6% of the variance in intention beyond the components of the theory of planned behavior (9% when past behavior was also controlled), and was related to behavior largely through intention (Rise et al., 2010).

text.text: Research on identity-based motivation adds that the specific identity that guides action at a given moment depends on cues in the immediate situation, and that these cues can operate subtly (Oyserman, 2009).

text.text: Together, this work suggests that a message cueing a valued identity could strengthen intention, and through intention, behavior.
Identity has also become a focus of health behavior research more broadly and brief identity cues can shift health choices.

For example, when junk food and drinking were presented as markers of a social group that students did not want to signal, students chose less junk food and reported drinking less alcohol (Berger & Rand, 2008).

text.text: Qualitative studies of weight loss, addiction recovery, and smoking cessation suggest that lasting change is accompanied and sustained by gradual shifts in identity (Epiphaniou & Ogden, 2010; Kearney & O'Sullivan, 2003; Meijer et al., 2020).

text.text: Deliberately changing identity has proven harder.

A writing exercise in which daily smokers imagined themselves as someone in the process of quitting produced only a marginal increase in quitter self-identity and no change in quit intentions or behavior (Meijer et al., 2018).

text.text: Noun-based framing is among the lightest-touch ways to cue identity.
Specifically, describing a preference with a noun rather than a verb leads people to see it as stronger and more stable (Walton & Banaji, 2004).

text.text: Despite identity framing having salience in the health context, to our knowledge it has not been tested on meditation nor other wellness practices in digital field experiments.
Testing noun framing among existing meditation listeners also allows a test of competing predictions about prior engagement.
If identity framing works best when the identity feels valued and attainable, it should be most effective among the most engaged listeners.

text.text: In the present study, we conducted a randomized field experiment with 3,000 existing listeners of a popular meditation teacher on Spotify who had varying degrees of engagement with the teacher.
Participants were sent an in-app message that framed meditation either as an identity ("Be a meditator today") or as a behavior ("Meditate today"), with otherwise identical content.
We tested whether identity framing increased message click-through (H1) and listening to the teacher's meditation content during the treatment period (H2).
We also explored whether prior listening volume moderated the effect of framing (RQ1).
The specific hypotheses and research questions are as follows: • H1: An identity-framed message will yield a higher click-through rate than a non-identity-framed message.
• H2: During the messaging treatment period, an identity-framed message will yield more listening to the meditation content than a non-identity-framed message.
• RQ1: Does prior listening volume moderate the effect of identity framing on message click-through?
By testing these hypotheses and exploring this research question, the present study can contribute to the often conflicting body of existing work in a new context, meditation.

Additionally, the findings can help theorists understand how identity theory cues may or may not be initiated, as well as help meditation content designers understand whether identity framing via messaging offers a clear opportunity for driving engagement.

To qualify to participate in the study, individuals needed to have listened to at least 1 minute of content provided by a popular meditation teacher using the Spotify app between August 27 and September 26, 2026.
Additional qualifications included being aged 18 years or older and residing in the United States.
Fieldwork was conducted from September 29 to October 4, 2026.
A random sample of 3,000 people was drawn from the eligible pool and randomly assigned to two conditions.

text.text: All meditation content in this study came from a single teacher's long-running mindfulness podcast, a large audio catalog that is freely available to the public.
The same catalog was used to determine eligibility and was where participants were sent if they clicked the message.
It contains two types of content: guided meditations and teachings, which are instructional talks and reflections meant to support practice.

The approach is mainly mindfulness-based, with a strong emphasis on self-compassion (e.g., attending to the breath and body, cultivating present-moment awareness, and working with difficult emotions).
Most episodes run 20 to 90 minutes.
Over more than a decade, the catalog has grown to more than 1,500 recordings, with new episodes typically at least weekly.
As the primary experimental intervention, participants were assigned to receive one of two potential messages to encourage them to listen to meditation content.
One message was the treatment condition and the other the control condition.

The treatment condition message, which was intended to cue the identity framing, included the headline "Be a meditator today" with the subtext "Practice mindfulness and meditation on Spotify with an expert teacher".
The control condition included the headline "Meditate today" with the same subtext as the treatment condition, "Practice mindfulness and meditation on Spotify with an expert teacher".
Both messages included two buttons, which were "Take me there!"
and "No thanks".
By tapping "Take me there!", participants were redirected to the popular meditation teacher's content on Spotify, from which qualified them to participate in the study.
By tapping "No thanks", the banner message was dismissed.
People could also dismiss the banner message by tapping an "X" on the top right side of the banner message or by swiping the banner message upward.
Tapping "No thanks", 'the "X", and swiping away the message were all treated equally as a message dismissal.
See Figure 1 for the banners used.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for the banners used.

text.text: The messages were served in the Spotify mobile app and were triggered when people in the sample visited the app's homepage.
The message type and call-to-action from this campaign are similar to the various types of in-app messages and notifications that Spotify users are accustomed to receiving.
The primary measure for H1 is the message click through rate.
This is calculated based on the number of people who clicked the "Take me there" button, which serves as the numerator in the click through rate for each test cell.
The total number of users in each test cell is the denominator in this calculation and serves as the intent to treat (ITT) measure for the click through rate.

Some people who were included in each of the treatment and control conditions may not have actually seen the message, which could have happened for a few reasons, such as if the person did not use the Spotify mobile app or whether they did not visit the home page of the app.
In the treatment, 74.6% of users saw the banner message and 69.7% of users in the control saw the banner message (χ²(1) = 8.64, p = .003).
This is a post-randomization effect and introduces a selection bias, and there are statistically significant differences between the treatment and control on this measure.
However, assessing the number of people who clicked on the message among people who saw the message is useful to understand and contextualize the results of the study.
Consequently, in addition to the primary ITT analysis we also assess the CTR using message impressions count (i.e., people who actually saw the message) in each test group as the denominator.
The primary measure for H2 is minutes spent listening to the teacher's content during the treatment period.
To preserve randomization, this is calculated for all assigned users, with users who did not listen assigned 0 minutes.
As secondary, non-randomized analyses, we compare the same outcome among users who viewed the message and among users who clicked it.
RQ1 explores whether heavier or lighter listeners of meditation content from the teacher included in the study interacts with the test condition.
In other words, do heavier or lighter listeners respond to the treatment or control message differently.
To define these groups, we used the median minutes spent listening to the meditation teacher during the pre-study qualification period to split heavier and lighter listeners.
Analyses were conducted in Python using pandas, SciPy, and statsmodels.
H1 was tested with a chi-square test of independence comparing the proportion of users who clicked in each condition.
All assigned users (ITT) formed the primary analysis.
H2 was tested with two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests because listening minutes were highly skewed and zero-inflated.
For the more exploratory RQ1, we fit a logistic regression using clicks from condition, engagement group, and their interaction, with the interaction term testing moderation.
As a robustness check, the model was refit with prior listening minutes as a continuous predictor (log-transformed).
A sensitivity analysis was conducted to determine the smallest effects the study could reliably detect.

With 1,529 and 1,471 participants per condition and a control click-through rate of 8.2%, the study had 80% power (α = .05, two-sided) to detect a difference in click-through rate of 3.0 percentage points (Cohen's h = 0.10), equivalent to a 37% relative increase.

For listening, the study had 80% power (α = .05, two-sided) to detect a difference of 4.6 percentage points in the proportion of users who listened during the treatment period (25.2% in the control condition).
Because listening minutes were heavily zero-inflated and analyzed with a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, this estimate is approximate.

This study tested whether framing meditation as an identity ("Be a meditator today") rather than a behavior ("Meditate today") would increase engagement among existing listeners of a meditation teacher.
It did not.
Click-through rates were virtually identical across conditions (8.2% in both).
Identity framing also did not increase listening during the treatment period among all assigned users, and the secondary comparisons among viewers and among clickers pointed the same way.
These results add a new domain to a growing body of null findings for noun-based identity framing.

text.text: The present study was designed with those conditions in mind.

Participants were existing listeners of a meditation teacher, meditation is a private behavior that most people regard as desirable, and the identity of "meditator" should be both plausible and appealing to this audience.
That identity framing still had no detectable effect makes it harder to attribute the broader pattern of null findings to unfavorable contexts.
At the same time, a single study in one setting cannot rule out a small effect, or an effect that depends on conditions this study did not capture.

The reasoned action approach offers a way to consider where the pathway from message to behavior may have broken down (although the present data cannot distinguish among the possibilities because beliefs, identity, and intention were not measured).
First, the noun may not have changed the beliefs that were salient when participants decided whether to act.

text.text: Future studies that measure identity salience, beliefs, and intention after exposure could determine which of these links fails.
Neither competing prediction about prior engagement was supported: identity framing was ineffective among both lighter and heavier listeners, and prior listening did not predict clicking.
However, prior listening is only a rough proxy for habit, and the moderation test had limited power to detect differences between groups.
For platforms that use messages to encourage meditation, rephrasing a call to action in identity terms is unlikely to improve engagement on its own.
Messages that address the beliefs that hold people back, tested before being deployed at scale, are a more promising route (Bowen et al., 2025).

text.text: There are several important limitations of this study to be considered: • The study was conducted on a single digital platform (Spotify) and includes only a single meditation teacher, which limits the broader generalizability of the findings.
Spotify may be unique in that it primarily offers music, podcast, and audiobook content and is not broadly considered a digital mental health services provider.
• Participants were mostly women (72%), U.S.-based, and already engaged with the meditation teacher's content.
• Listening time has been used as a proxy for practice, which may not have necessarily been what users were doing while listening to the content.
• The single, short message may also not have been adequate to instantiate one's identity as a meditator, although previous research in other contexts has suggested as much.
• Additionally, the mechanism that the message was intended to evoke was untested.
Without measures of identity, beliefs, or intention, the study cannot show whether the message activated a meditator identity at all.
• Finally, more treatment than control participants saw the message (74.6% vs.
69.7%), so analyses among viewers and clickers are not randomized comparisons.
Future studies could explore in more depth the specific mechanisms that activate identity in the meditation context.
From an identity framing messaging perspective, future researchers might strive to understand where the pathway from message to behavior breaks down.
They could also test identity framing among people new to meditation, for whom deliberate motivation should matter more, and compare identity framing with messages that target specific beliefs.

Framing meditation as an identity rather than a behavior did not increase engagement among existing listeners of a meditation teacher, even in a setting that arguably met the conditions proponents of noun framing have identified.
